problem: Prior map-based NL navigation datasets (HCRC, SAIL, TTW) use small, simple symbolic worlds with a small fixed entity set known in advance, bypassing the complexity of real urban navigation (long paths, many unseen entities).
motivation: Real urban navigation requires grounding instructions to a dense map with abundant unseen entities of different types, and long routes are vulnerable to error propagation. A realistic benchmark evaluated on the full route (not just the final position) is needed to study this.
key_idea: Introduce the RUN task and dataset (2515 instructions aligned to routes on OpenStreetMap Manhattan maps) and a seq2seq baseline with entity abstraction, attention over words and world-state, and a constantly updated world-state.
insight: Ablations show each component matters: replacing unseen entities with typed variables (CGA to CGAE) helps handle OOV entities (sentence accuracy 43.68 to 46.01), and adding world-state to attention (CGAEW) gives the largest jump (62.37 sentence, 10.45 paragraph). Paragraph accuracy stays low (10.45 vs human 81.12), so long-route error propagation and unmarked or generic entities (blocks, intersections, traffic lights) remain hard.
method: RUN dataset: MTurk workers wrote route descriptions between two self-chosen landmarks and pinned the route sentence by sentence on OSM; three disjoint testers verified each route, giving human-performance estimates and filtering bad routes. Maps cover 3 Manhattan regions of 0.5 km² each, split into 11.132 m tiles.

Task formulation: input is a tiled map, a start point and an instruction paragraph; output is the full sequence of coordinates. Actions are TURN (left/right/around), WALK (one tile along the street) and END.
Encoder/Decoder with attention (CGA): biLSTM encodes each sentence and an LSTM decoder generates actions, with beam search (size 4) and GNMT length normalization.
Entity abstraction (CGAE): phrases naming unseen entities are replaced with typed, order-numbered variables (X1, Y1) before encoding; numbering resets per utterance.

World-State Processor (CGAEW): maps variables to map entities and builds two vectors, entities at the current position and entities on the path ahead. These are fed into the attention scores over words and are updated every step.
Execution system: executes each predicted action in both training and testing to obtain the next position.

setting.backbone: biLSTM encoder + LSTM decoder with attention (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: RUN dataset: 2515 instructions / 389 paragraphs over 3 Manhattan maps; 3-fold cross-validation with 2 maps for train (90%) / val (10%) and 1 map for test
setting.observation: symbolic OpenStreetMap tile map with entity labels (name, type, is_building, house number) and walkable streets; text instructions
setting.action_space: discrete TURN / WALK (one tile) / END on the tile grid
setting.simulator: custom OSM tile-based map environment (no visual simulator)

numbers.backbone: biLSTM encoder-decoder with attention, entity abstraction and world-state
numbers.extra: 3-fold cross-validation, size-weighted average over test maps; success = final position within 5 tiles (sentences also require the correct heading)
numbers.evidence: Table 4 (Bounds on Accuracy for Sentences\Paragraphs): CGAEW 62.37 (3.11)\10.45

numbers.backbone: biLSTM encoder-decoder with attention and entity abstraction

numbers.extra: ablation without entity abstraction or world-state; 3-fold cross-validation

numbers_note: Human accuracy (81.12 on paragraphs) and the NO-MOVE, RANDOM and JUMP baselines are reported, but they are not the paper's own models and are omitted from the numbers.
results: The full CGAEW model reaches 62.37% sentence accuracy and 10.45% paragraph accuracy, beating CGAE (46.01 / 6.17), CGA (43.68 / 0.26) and the simple baselines (best NO-MOVE 30.3 / 0.3). It is still far below human paragraph accuracy of 81.12%.
limitations: Paragraph-level accuracy remains very low (10.45%) because errors propagate along long routes.
The world-state cannot capture abstract, unmarked entities (blocks, intersections) or generic ones (traffic lights).
Small dataset (3 maps, 389 paragraphs), no visual signals, and the FACE/VERIFY actions were not made useful.
builds_on: Iyer et al. 2017 / Suhr et al. 2018 entity abstraction
